_schema: One station, in the shape M3 fixed. M6 adds `when` on a canvas: the ISO date behind the holder's own words, so tools/station.py can ask whether a canvas is inside its station's span.
title: Auvers
_canvases: Five canvases from the last nine weeks, in the order he painted them, around one standpoint like station 4. Every treatment here is the measurement's -- `treatment` is null on all five and tools/place.py decides whether each is a plain or a wall. That is the point of building this station ninth: by now the test has been run on twenty canvases and the piece can afford to let it answer without an override anywhere.

canvases.title: The Church at Auvers
canvases.note: 74.5 by 94 cm, from the Ministry of Culture's Joconde record for RF 1951-42, which is the museum's own catalogue published by the state -- the Orsay itself answers a plain request with 403, which paintings/CREDITS.md has recorded since M4. DESIGN 7 wants the church with its two paths splitting around it and this is the canvas that has them. And it measures **18.3x** on the level-against-upright cut, the strongest horizon at this station and the seventh in a collection of thirty, above the Sower's 11.1x and the Wheatfield with Crows' 15.2x -- which is not what you would guess about a portrait-format canvas of a building. What the test has found is the line where the two paths part from the grass, and it is right: this canvas is a place, and the church is standing in it.

canvases.title: Thatched Cottages at Cordeville
canvases.note: The accession number is corrected here and in tools/sources.tsv: this file and the source table both said RF 1954-15 from M0b, and Joconde's record for RF 1954-15 is Le jardin du docteur Gachet, a portrait-format canvas 73 by 52 cm. Cordeville is RF 1954-14, 73 by 92. The scan is 1.264 wide to tall, which is Cordeville and not the garden, so what was wrong was the number in the file and never the picture. It measures 10.0x and lifts.

canvases.title: Daubigny's Garden
canvases.note: Measures 0.9x on the level-against-upright cut -- no horizon at all, lower than a self-portrait -- so it is a wall and it stands where the field of view says the painter stood. A garden seen close is not a place you can walk into and the test says so without being told.

canvases.title: Stairway at Auvers
canvases.note: Measures 7.6x and lifts. 70.5 by 50 cm, from the Saint Louis Art Museum's own object page.

canvases.title: Wheatfield under Thunderclouds
canvases.note: 101.3 by 50.4 cm, a double square, and the weakest scan in the whole set at 39 px/cm against the 120 the pipeline works at. paintings/CREDITS.md has said since M0b that the museum has published nothing better. What that costs is visible: the stroke count here is what a canvas looks like when the extractor is resolving marks it cannot quite see.

_ground: The Oise valley rather than the Crau: a shorter dome and a smaller swell than station 4, because the fields above Auvers roll and are bounded, and DESIGN 7 asks for cool green and grey-blue rather than heat.

caption.title: Auvers
caption.sub: May to July 1890. Five canvases from the last nine weeks, and not one treatment here is an override: tools/place.py is left to say which of them are places and which are walls, and it says a garden is not a place.

_volume: M6 sets this. DESIGN 15's volume question was open from M3 to M6 with three possible answers written down, and the one that turned out to be true is the third: the instrument was wrong. `nearEdge` counts time spent within half a metre of the boundary, which any walker with a net forward drift accumulates simply by arriving there -- forty seconds at 1.45 m/s is 58 metres, so M3's sweep answering '50 by 40' was measuring the walk and not the volume. `pressing` counts time spent holding a key that would go further out while the ground takes the body back: trying to leave rather than standing at the edge. Swept at station 4 with the `look` walker, which is the only one of the three that stops and turns and looks: 27.0% at 12 by 7, 20.6% at 18 by 11, **12.7% at 26 by 16** and 0.0% at 40 by 25. So this is the first size in the sweep that comes under the fifth M3 pre-registered, and it is two to three times the old slab rather than the seven M3 feared. What it costs is a thin far field: the plain is a quarter of its own density by six metres out and this walks to twenty-six. `wander` still fails here at 49.6% and always will, because an amble in a straight line for forty seconds is not something any bounded place absorbs.
